4dc33674e3ba0c79:
**Split, so not a fusion** (`soup.split`, E). Bijective translations turn both bridges into one-operation laws: law 1 makes every left translation of · a bijection, and law 2 does the same for the right translations of ∘. E proves both directions of the equivalence with V(·) plus V^op(∘), where V = {x·(x·y) = y, (x·y)·y = y} (ETP 16 and 28) and V^op = {(x∘y)∘y = x, x∘(x∘y) = x}.

Nearest literature: bikei (involutory biquandles; Nelson and Rosenfield, arXiv:1603.02719, Definition 1). Their laws (ii.i) (x b y) b y = x and (ii.ii) (x a y) a y = x also make translations involutions. The candidate is not a bikei fragment: their Example 1 bikei (x a y = x b y = σ(x), σ an involution) fails x·(x·y) = y under either assignment of the operations. Searches (22 Nov 2026) found no source for V.
8a5129571ae99c51:
**An idempotent left quasigroup in disguise.** E proves both directions of the equivalence with {x·(y∘x) = y, (x·y)∘x = y, x·x = x, (x·y)·y = y, x·(y·x) = y·x}. So y∘x is the left division x\y of ·, and the theory is the variety of idempotent left quasigroups (·, \) satisfying x·(y·x) = y·x (ETP 333) and (x·y)·y = y (ETP 28). `soup.relabel` finds the same thing, up to relabelling, against the named left quasigroups. Rank 9 (`977c3603`) is the same without (x·y)·y = y.

Not a rack: E saturates against left distributivity. It is also not a twisted Ward left quasigroup ((x·y)·(x·z) = (y·y)·(y·z); Stanovský and Vojtěchovský, arXiv:2002.02854) and not a cycle set ((x·y)·(x·z) = (y·x)·(y·z), Rump 2005). The 3-element model is still a quandle: L₀ = L₁ = id, L₂ = (0 1). The affine models x·y = a·x + b·y with a² = 0 and b = (1+a)⁻¹, for instance 2x + 3y on ℤ/4, are Alexander quandles. Left quasigroups as a variety, with their commutator theory: Bonatto, *Nilpotent left quasigroups*, arXiv:2204.04448. Searches (22 Nov 2026) found no source that names left quasigroups with x(yx) = yx.

Verdict: a subvariety of a named variety (left quasigroups), cut out by two one-operation laws. It is a candidate for a name only if those two identities matter in the left-quasigroup or Yang–Baxter literature, and we found no sign that they do.

No associativity and no commutativity: E saturates against both. Nearest literature: skew lattices and their absorption variants (Leech, *Noncommutative Lattices*, 2020), which are associative. 2dc2750850548a58: **No named theory implied** under any of the 8 relabellings (`soup.relabel`). By E's convergent presentation (12 rules), · alone satisfies x·x = x, x·(y·x) = x (ETP 10), (x·y)·x = x (ETP 25), (x·y)·y = x·y (ETP 378) and x·(x·y) = x·y (ETP 323). ∘ alone satisfies only x∘x = x. Math. J. 48 (1998)). We did not read these papers, and the results show no second operation. No source found for the theory.
10c98c4b5db2a4bd: **Transpose-orthogonality with a decoder, plus absorption.** E proves both directions of the equivalence with B ∪ {(x∘y)·x = x, x·(y∘x) = x, (x·y)∘x = x, x∘(y·x) = x}, where B = {(x·y)∘(y·x) = x, (x∘y)·(y∘x) = x}. B says that φ(x,y) = (x·y, y·x) is a bijection of A² whose inverse is (u,v) ↦ (u∘v, v∘u). So · is orthogonal to its transpose as a binary operation, and ∘ decodes the pair. B alone does not imply idempotence or the absorptions (E saturates), so the absorptions are what the search added. The four absorptions are one law, (x∘y)·x = x, with its images under the three dualities. All four are needed: for each proper subset, E saturates against the rest. For Latin squares, orthogonality to the transpose is self-orthogonality. Self-orthogonal Latin squares exist for every order except 2, 3 and 6 (Brayton, Coppersmith and Hoffman, Bull. AMS 80 (1974)). Here · is never Latin in a non-degenerate model: the theory proves x·(x·y) = x·y, so a bijective left translation would be the identity, and · would be the right projection. With ∘ = ·, B becomes Schröder's second law (xy)(yx) = x. According to the search results, that is one of Belousov's identities that make a quasigroup orthogonal to a parastrophe; we did not read the sources. Non-degenerate models up to isomorphism (Mace4): none on 2 or 3 elements, 2 on 4, 14 on 5, at least 214 on 6 (the search hit its cap), all idempotent. B alone has 38 on 3 elements (an earlier version of this note said 40; Mace4 and a complete enumeration of the 3^9 tables both give 38). In the smallest one, x·y keeps the high bit of y, and its low bit is x₀ + x₁(1 + y₁) (elements as bit pairs). E saturates against associativity and commutativity of either operation. Searches (22 Nov 2026) found no source for B as a two-operation variety, nor for B with these absorptions. Post hoc (`notes/10c98c4b_checks.py`, E both ways): under B each absorption is equivalent to a one-operation law, (x∘y)·x = x to x·(x·y) = x·y and so on, so the theory says that · is orthogonal to its transpose and that every left and right translation of · and of its decoder ∘ is idempotent. With ∘ = ·, rectangular bands are models. **B is prior art:** it says that · is Δ-bijective and ∘ is its dual operation. Dehornoy, Adv. Math. 282 (2015), arXiv:1403.3019, §1, has the 'involutivity laws' equivalent to the bijectivity of (s,t) ↦ (s∗t, t∗s) for arbitrary operations (the same lemma is in Foundations of Garside Theory, Lemma XIII.1.28). Bonatto, Kinyon, Stanovský and Vojtěchovský, arXiv:1910.02148, §2.5, Lemma 2.10, has it too. The idea is credited to Rump, Adv. Math. 193 (2005) 40–55. That literature combines it with the right-cyclic law or bijective left translations. No non-degenerate model of this theory is a left or right quasigroup, and none of the 16 on 4 and 5 elements gives a Yang–Baxter solution through r(x,y) = (x·y, y·x). No source found for the full theory. Literature memo, with the sources read and those still to read: `notes/10c98c4b.md`.

d1e1c31f6ca1062c: **An absorption-type algebra without associativity.** It implies the absorption pair with ∘ reversed, x·(y∘x) = x and (x·y)∘x = x (`soup.relabel`, E). E's convergent presentation (10 rules) gives both operations idempotent. · alone satisfies x·(y·x) = x (ETP 10) and (x·y)·y = x·y (ETP 378), and ∘ alone satisfies (x∘y)∘x = x (ETP 25) and x∘(x∘y) = x∘y (ETP 323). The bridges are x·(y∘x) = x, (x·y)∘x = x, (x∘y)·y = x∘y and x∘(x·y) = x·y. E finds no implication either way, under any of the 8 relabellings, with `1ca933c1`, `3078949b`, `87137d88`, `2dc27508` or `69dfbd8e`. Not split (`soup.split` found a finite certificate). E saturates against associativity and commutativity of either operation, and against (x·y)·z = x·z and x·(y·z) = x·z (and the same for ∘). With both operations associative, E proves that each is a rectangular band, so the associative models are pairs of rectangular bands. With · commutative the theory is trivial: x·(y·x) = x and (x·y)·y = x·y then give x·y = y, and so x = y (hand proof). That rules out commutative hosts such as weakly associative lattices and bisemilattices. According to a delegated lookup of Leech's *Noncommutative Lattices* (2020, pp. 29–32), x·(y∘x) = x and (x·y)∘x = x are two of Leech's skew*-lattice absorption laws, and his noncommutative lattices are always associative. A bisemilattice “co-absorption law” of the same shape as (x∘y)·y = x∘y appears in Godowski, Demonstratio Math. 25 (1992) (review only). No source found for the theory (22 Nov 2026: web, zbMATH, the lookup). It reads as a nonassociative generalisation of pairs of rectangular bands.
3e068fa6f6e686f6: **Half of the Δ-bijective core, plus idempotence.** E's convergent presentation has 3 rules: (x∘y)·(y∘x) = y, x·x = x and x∘x = x. The first says that (x,y) ↦ (x∘y, y∘x) has the left inverse (u,v) ↦ (v·u, u·v). So ∘ is Δ-injective, with · as the transposed decoder. In a finite model, injective means bijective, so every finite model also satisfies (y·x)∘(x·y) = x: it is a Δ-bijective pair (Bonatto, Kinyon, Stanovský and Vojtěchovský, arXiv:1910.02148, Lemma 2.10), relabelled, with both operations idempotent. That law is not an equational consequence: the presentation is convergent and does not join its two sides, so some infinite model fails it. `10c98c4b`, relabelled (rev∘, rev·, and either with swap), implies this theory (E). A finite-versus-infinite gap of the same kind as the one-sided quasigroup laws (CLAUDE.md, facts confirmed). Not split; implies no named theory under the 8 relabellings. With ∘ = ·, the first law is Stein's third law x = (y◇x)◇(x◇y) (ETP 167, checked in the ETP list), so the specialisation is idempotent groupoids with Stein's third law (ETP 3 and 167). The Stein-third-law literature found is about quasigroups (J. D. H. Smith 2014; Griggs and Kozlik 2021, reviews only). According to the lookup, Shcherbacov (arXiv:1509.00796) says these identities still need a separate study for groupoids. The nearest documented finite-versus-infinite gap is Rump's: finite cycle sets are non-degenerate, infinite ones need not be (Rump 2005, as cited in arXiv:2001.10774). No source found for the two-operation theory or for injective-only Δ in groupoids (22 Nov 2026).
